notes.meaning: Jesus finished his teaching in Galilee and set out toward Jerusalem by traveling through the region east of the Jordan River. This journey marked the close of his long public ministry in Galilee. He was now beginning his final journey toward the cross.

Great crowds of people followed Jesus as he traveled, and he healed their sick along the way. Jesus never grew tired of helping people in distress. Wherever he went, he showed God's kingdom through both his preaching and his acts of mercy.

Some Pharisees came to Jesus trying to trap him with a difficult question about divorce. Jewish teachers at that time were divided, with some allowing divorce only for adultery and others permitting it for almost any dislike. The leaders hoped Jesus would pick a side and make enemies either with the crowds or with local rulers.

Jesus answered their trick question by pointing back to the creation story in Genesis. He reminded them that in the beginning, the Creator made human beings male and female. True marriage was designed by God right from the start, before any human laws were made.

Jesus quoted Scripture to show that a man must leave his parents and be joined closely to his wife. Marriage creates a completely new household where two individuals become one flesh. God designed this bond to be closer and more lasting than even the tie between parents and children.

Because a husband and wife become one flesh, they are no longer two separate lives before God. Marriage is not merely a human agreement, but a holy bond created by God himself. Therefore, no human being has the right to tear apart what God has united.

The Pharisees objected by asking why Moses commanded a husband to give his wife a divorce certificate. They thought Jesus was speaking against the law of Moses. In reality, they were treating a legal safeguard meant to protect women as if it were a command to end marriages.

Jesus explained that Moses permitted divorce only because the people had hard, stubborn hearts. The law was a concession to limit cruelty, not God's original goal for husband and wife. God's true plan from the start was for marriage to last a lifetime.

Jesus stated that whoever divorces his wife and marries someone else commits adultery, unless the divorce is caused by sexual unfaithfulness. Marital unfaithfulness breaks the sacred union of marriage. Outside of this grave sin, God calls husbands and wives to stay faithful to their vows.

differ.view: The Westminster Confession teaches that when one spouse commits adultery, the innocent partner has a biblical right to get a divorce. That partner is then entirely free to remarry, just as if the unfaithful spouse had died.

The Assemblies of God teaches that Jesus gave a narrow exception for marital unfaithfulness, because sexual sin breaks the marriage covenant (a holy promise made before God). When this happens, the innocent spouse may divorce and remarry without being guilty of adultery.

The Lutheran Church—Missouri Synod teaches that sexual unfaithfulness is the only ground Jesus gives that allows an innocent spouse to divorce and remarry without committing adultery. However, the church emphasizes that Jesus gave this exception to forbid all other reasons for divorce, not to encourage couples to separate.

The United Methodist Church affirms that marriage is meant to last for life, but it recognizes that divorce can be a necessary step when a relationship becomes abusive or damaged beyond repair. In its official teachings, a past divorce does not bar a person from remarrying or serving in the church.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Catholic Church teaches that a valid, consummated marriage cannot be dissolved, meaning spouses may separate if sexual unfaithfulness occurs, but neither may remarry while the other lives.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: The Orthodox Church permits divorce and remarriage in tragic cases like unfaithfulness, viewing it as a pastoral mercy when a marriage has ended in reality.

notes.meaning: The disciples were shocked by how strict Jesus made the marriage bond compared to the easy divorce rules of their day. They told Jesus that if a man could never leave an unhappy marriage, it would be better never to marry at all. They felt that lifelong commitment sounded more like a trap than a blessing.

Jesus answered that remaining unmarried is not a rule for everyone. Living happily without marriage is a special gift from God given only to certain people. Most people are called to marry, while others receive the grace to live single lives.

Jesus explained that some people cannot marry because of how they were born or because of physical harm caused by others. Others choose to remain single on purpose so they can devote all their energy to serving God's kingdom. Single life is an honorable calling, but only for those who are given the ability to embrace it.

People brought little children and babies to Jesus so he could place his hands on them and pray. The disciples rebuked the parents, thinking children were an unimportant distraction from Jesus' serious work. They did not yet understand how much Jesus values the smallest and weakest.

Jesus told his disciples to stop turning the children away and let them come to him. He declared that God's kingdom belongs to people who are like these little ones. To enter God's family, adults must come with the simple trust and humility of a child.

differ.view: Many Baptists believe this passage shows Christ's love for children, but does not support baptizing infants before they make a personal profession of faith.
Anglicans teach that Jesus welcoming infants shows that children of believers belong to God's covenant and should receive infant baptism.

notes.meaning: Jesus placed his hands on the children, blessed them warmly, and then left that place. His loving touch showed that even the youngest individuals are deeply cared for by God. No person is too small or insignificant to receive the Savior's blessing.

A young ruler ran up and asked Jesus what good deed he needed to do to earn eternal life. He was wealthy, eager, and morally upright, but he thought heaven could be won by human achievement. He wanted to know which extra heroic work would guarantee his salvation.

Jesus asked the man why he asked about what is good, reminding him that God alone is truly good. Jesus pointed him toward the commandments of God's law. By giving this answer, Jesus began showing the man that God's perfect goodness is a standard no sinner can meet on their own.

When the young man asked which commandments were required, Jesus quoted rules about loving other people, such as not murdering, not committing adultery, not stealing, not lying, and honoring parents. He summed them up with the command to love one's neighbor as oneself. Jesus used these commandments to test how well the man actually loved the people around him.

The young man replied that he had kept all these rules since he was a boy, but he still asked what he was missing. Even though he had lived an outwardly moral life, his conscience was not at peace. He sensed deep down that his good deeds had not satisfied the holy requirements of God.

Jesus challenged him to sell everything he owned, give the money to the poor, and follow him. Jesus was not saying that giving away money buys a ticket to heaven, but was exposing the man's secret idol. The young man loved his wealth more than he loved God or his neighbor.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some prosperity preachers claim God promises material wealth to faithful Christians, whereas Jesus taught that wealth can easily become an idol that hinders discipleship.

notes.meaning: When the young man heard what Jesus asked, he walked away filled with grief because he had great wealth. When forced to choose between his possessions and Jesus, he chose his money. His sorrow showed that he valued temporary earthly treasures above eternal life.

Jesus turned to his disciples and told them how hard it is for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven. Having plenty of money makes people feel safe and self-reliant, blinding them to their spiritual poverty. It is very hard for wealthy people to humble themselves and rely only on God's mercy.

Jesus repeated his warning with a memorable picture, saying it is easier for a large camel to squeeze through the eye of a sewing needle than for a rich person to be saved. He was describing something that is humanly impossible. Anyone who trusts in money cannot enter the narrow gate of God's kingdom.

The disciples were completely shocked and asked who could ever be saved. In their culture, wealth was commonly viewed as a sure sign that God was pleased with someone. If even the most successful and blessed people could not enter the kingdom, they wondered how ordinary people had any hope.

Jesus looked straight at his disciples and said that while salvation is impossible for human effort, all things are possible with God. No person can save themselves, no matter how much wealth or virtue they possess. Salvation is a miraculous gift of God's power changing the human heart.

Peter spoke up and pointed out that he and the other disciples had left their homes and livelihoods to follow Jesus. He then asked what they would receive in return. Unlike the rich young ruler, they had obeyed Jesus' call, but Peter was still wondering about their future reward.

Jesus promised his disciples that in the future renewal of all creation, when he sits on his glorious throne, they will sit on twelve thrones ruling over the twelve tribes of Israel. God will reward their loyal service by letting them share in the glory of his kingdom. Faithful discipleship always leads to honor in the age to come.

Jesus gave a broad promise to anyone who leaves family, home, or lands for his sake. He assured them that God will give them back a hundred times as much through spiritual blessings and the church family, along with eternal life in heaven. No sacrifice made for Jesus will ever be wasted or forgotten.

Jesus concluded by warning that many who are first in this world will end up last, while the last will be first. God does not measure success the way humans do with money, prestige, or status. Those who are humble and overlooked for Christ's sake will be lifted up to the highest places in God's kingdom.
